phase1.intro:
The storefront is open. Five units ago this started as a single blueprint — one class, one object. Here's the full arc, front to back.

Where do you want to start the recap?

topics.buttonText: How did Units 1 through 4 build up to this?
dialogue: [[term:Unit 1]] built the blueprint itself — syntax, variables, control flow, class vs object. [[term:Unit 2]] extended that into families of blueprints — inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces. [[term:Unit 3]] was about trust — catching, reporting, recovering from things going wrong. [[term:Unit 4]] stocked the shelves and hired help — Collections and Threads.

stickyNote.definition: Unit 1: syntax and blueprints. Unit 2: inheritance/polymorphism families. Unit 3: exceptions and I/O trust. Unit 4: Collections and Threads at scale.

topics.buttonText: How did all of Unit 5's pieces fit together?
dialogue: Stage and Scene gave the storefront a building and window display. Layouts arranged the shelves, Controls stocked them, Event handling made touching them mean something. CSS painted the shop, FXML let you redesign without touching code, Binding put self-updating price tags, ListView/TableView built the catalog board, Alerts gave it a voice, Animation made things move — and the mini-app put it all under one roof.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏬 building, shelves, controls, and everything that brings them to life
stickyNote.definition: Stage/Scene (building), Layouts (shelves), Controls (stock), Events, CSS, FXML, Binding, ListView/TableView, Alerts, Animation — all combined in the mini-app.

topics.buttonText: What actually transfers to other frameworks from here?
dialogue: [[fun:From here, the same core ideas keep showing up in bigger shapes]] — Spring Framework does dependency injection and web handling on the same OOP fundamentals; Android's View system will look structurally familiar. [[key:None of what you learned here was toolkit-specific — it was how software gets organized, and that transfers]].

stickyNote.flavor: 🌉 the organizing ideas outlast the specific toolkit
stickyNote.definition: The OOP and organizing patterns from this course transfer beyond JavaFX — to Spring, Android, and enterprise Java, which reuse the same fundamentals.

phase1.openingDialogue: The storefront is open — five units of blueprints, families, trust, scale, and now a real interface, all built on ideas that transfer beyond JavaFX. 🏬

phase2.explanation:
No broken code — one last conceptual lesson to close out the course. A few honest closing notes instead.

[[key:the fastest way to lose everything you just built is to stop using it]] — the next project you build, even a small one, is worth more than rereading these lessons a second time. Pick something slightly beyond your comfort zone and let yourself get stuck on it; that's where the real learning happens, not in a lesson that already knows the answer.

[[warn:Java keeps moving]] — new language features land roughly every six months since Java 9's release cadence began, and a few of them (records, pattern matching, virtual threads) will look unfamiliar even against everything in this course. That's normal — a solid OOP foundation is what lets you pick up each new feature quickly, not a reason to feel behind.

phase3.openingDialogue: One final question! What's next in your Java journey? 🤔

mcq.question:
What is the recommended framework for building web applications with Java?

A) JavaFX
B) Swing
C) Spring Framework
D) Android SDK

Select the CORRECT answer.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Java has shipped a new major version roughly every six months since Java 9 (2017)]] — a deliberate shift away from the old multi-year release cycle, specifically so new language features could reach developers faster instead of waiting years for the next big bundled release.
